vignette:
Marlene is a fifty-year-old jeweler who has worked in her own small shop in the city’s downtown for nearly two decades. She is single and lives alone in a ground-floor apartment with a deadbolt she checks three times before bed. The assault happened on a Tuesday afternoon, just before closing. A man came in, looked at a few pieces, then pulled a knife and demanded she empty the case. She remembers his face clearly — the flat, impatient set of his mouth — but the moments after he grabbed her wrist are almost entirely blank. She knows she screamed, but the sound is gone. What she does recall, in fragments that arrive without warning, is the smell of his sweat and the cold metal of the blade pressed against her neck. Those pieces appear suddenly — while she is polishing a ring, or reaching for a tool — and then vanish before she can make sense of them. Other times she finds herself pushing the memory away deliberately, stopping it before it fully arrives, because she knows that if she lets it complete, she will feel nauseated for hours. After the memory had surfaced, even the most ordinary things — a kettle whistling, a door slamming — felt like warnings she couldn't afford to ignore.

What frightens Marlene most is not the memory itself but what it has done to her. She has come to believe that her reactions since that day show how poorly she handles things — that she is a lousy coper, that other people would have bounced back by now. This thought surfaces most sharply when she is triggered. If she hears a customer talk about losing a loved one, she feels a wave of shame: why can’t she move on from a few minutes of violence? The nausea that follows those conversations reinforces her sense of being contaminated, as though the assault left something inside her that cannot be washed away. She has begun to feel dead inside, emotionally numb, as if the only way to survive is to stop feeling altogether.

These negative appraisals feed directly into her constant sense of threat. Because she believes she is weak, Marlene is certain that the world is full of danger she cannot handle. She now scans for exits as soon as she enters any room — her own shop included. She has moved her workbench so it faces the door, and she notes every customer’s hands. Strangers who approach her in ordinary situations, like someone asking for directions on the street, make her heart race. She only feels safe in a very limited number of places: her apartment, her shop, and a friend’s house on the other side of town. And even within those safe zones, the threat never fully disappears. The act of scanning for exits sometimes triggers a sudden piece of memory — the flash of the knife — which then cycles back into more vigilance.

The offender himself is the most potent trigger. Once, a few months after the assault, she saw a man with the same build and same walk in the grocery store. She left her cart and walked out without buying anything. That one sighting kept her hypervigilant for days. Now, whenever she feels a spike of threat — a stranger stepping too close, a shadow in her peripheral vision — her mind immediately searches for offender cues. She has become convinced that she is on the verge of encountering him again, even though he was arrested and is still in custody.

After the assault, Marlene stopped working evenings. She lost two regular clients who preferred late appointments. Her hands, which were always steady, now tremble when she sets a stone. She sought help not because of the fear itself, but because she realized she had stopped wearing her own jewelry — pieces she once loved now felt wrong against her skin, as if she were still contaminated. She is afraid that she will never feel clean again, and she is hoping that therapy will give her a way to stop the cycle before her shop becomes the last place she can stand to be.

violations.explanation: The vignette does not depict that the intrusive memory causes or leads to triggers; instead, the memory appears spontaneously or is triggered by threat, not the other way around.

vignette_attempts.feedback:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Memory → Triggers: The vignette does not depict that the intrusive memory causes or leads to triggers; instead, the memory appears spontaneously or is triggered by threat, not the other way around.
  e.g. "After the memory had surfaced, even the most ordinary things — a kettle whistling, a door slamming — felt like warnings she couldn't afford to ignore."
  e.g. "The intrusive image left her scanning every room she entered, cataloguing exits, tracking faces, unable to switch off."
  e.g. "Because the memory came back so vividly, she began to see threads of it everywhere: in strangers' faces, in certain times of day, in the quality of winter light."
